{{Short description|Knot defined by parametric equations defining Lissajous curves}}
In [[knot theory]], a '''Lissajous knot''' is a [[knot (mathematics)|knot]] defined by [[parametric equations]] of the form

:<math>x = \cos(n_x t + \phi_x),\qquad  y = \cos(n_y t + \phi_y), \qquad  z = \cos(n_z t + \phi_z),</math>

[[Image:Lissajous 8 21 Knot.png|thumb|A Lissajous 8<sub>21</sub> knot]]
where <math>n_x</math>, <math>n_y</math>, and <math>n_z</math> are [[integer]]s and the [[phase shift]]s <math>\phi_x</math>, <math>\phi_y</math>, and <math>\phi_z</math> may be any [[real number]]s.<ref name="Bogle">{{cite journal |first1=M. G. V. |last1=Bogle |first2=J. E. |last2=Hearst |first3=V. F. R. |last3=Jones |first4=L. |last4=Stoilov |title=Lissajous knots |journal=Journal of Knot Theory and Its Ramifications |volume=3 |issue=2 |year=1994 |pages=121–140|doi=10.1142/S0218216594000095 }}</ref>

The projection of a Lissajous knot onto any of the three coordinate planes is a [[Lissajous curve]], and many of the properties of these knots are closely related to properties of Lissajous curves.

Replacing the cosine function in the parametrization by a [[triangle wave]] transforms every Lissajous
knot isotopically into a billiard curve inside a cube, the simplest case of so-called ''billiard knots''.
Billiard knots can also be studied in other domains, for instance in a cylinder<ref name="Cylinder">{{cite journal |first1=Christoph |last1=Lamm |first2=Daniel |last2=Obermeyer |title=Billiard knots in a cylinder |journal=Journal of Knot Theory and Its Ramifications |volume=8 |issue=3 |year=1999 |pages=353–366|bibcode=1998math.....11006L |arxiv=math/9811006 |doi=10.1142/S0218216599000225 |s2cid=17489206 }}</ref> or in a (flat) [[solid torus]] ([[Lissajous-toric knot]]).

== Form ==
Because a knot cannot be self-intersecting, the three integers <math>n_x, n_y, n_z</math> must be pairwise [[relatively prime]], and none of the quantities

:<math>n_x \phi_y - n_y \phi_x,\quad  n_y \phi_z - n_z \phi_y,\quad n_z \phi_x - n_x \phi_z</math>

may be an integer multiple of [[pi]].  Moreover, by making a substitution of the form <math>t' = t+c</math>, one may assume that any of the three phase shifts <math>\phi_x</math>, <math>\phi_y</math>, <math>\phi_z</math> is equal to zero.

== Examples ==
Here are some examples of Lissajous knots,<ref>{{cite book |last=Cromwell |first=Peter R. |title=Knots and links |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, UK |year=2004 |pages=13 |isbn=978-0-521-54831-1}}</ref> all of which have <math>\phi_z=0</math>:
<gallery  widths="180px">
Image:Lissajous 5_2 Knot.png|[[Three-twist knot]] <br> <math>(n_x,n_y,n_z)=(3,2,7)</math> <br> <math>(\phi_x,\phi_y)=(0.7,0.2)</math>
Image:Lissajous Stevedore Knot.png|[[Stevedore knot (mathematics)|Stevedore knot]] <br> <math>(n_x,n_y,n_z)=(3,2,5)</math> <br> <math>(\phi_x,\phi_y)=(1.5,0.2)</math>
Image:Lissajous Square Knot.png|[[Square knot (mathematics)|Square knot]] <br> <math>(n_x,n_y,n_z)=(3,5,7)</math> <br> <math>(\phi_x,\phi_y)=(0.7,1.0)</math>
Image:Lissajous 8_21 Knot.png|8<sub>21</sub> knot <br> <math>(n_x,n_y,n_z)=(3,4,7)</math> <br> <math>(\phi_x,\phi_y)=(0.1,0.7)</math>
</gallery>
There are infinitely many different Lissajous knots,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Lamm | first1 = C. | year = 1997 | title = There are infinitely many Lissajous knots | journal = Manuscripta Mathematica | volume = 93 | pages = 29–37 | doi=10.1007/BF02677455| s2cid = 123288245 }}</ref> and other examples with 10 or fewer [[crossing number (knot theory)|crossings]] include the 7<sub>4</sub> knot, the 8<sub>15</sub> knot, the 10<sub>1</sub> knot, the 10<sub>35</sub> knot, the 10<sub>58</sub> knot, and the composite knot 5<sub>2</sub><sup>*</sup>&nbsp;#&nbsp;5<sub>2</sub>,<ref name="Bogle"/> as well as the 9<sub>16</sub> knot, 10<sub>76</sub> knot, the 10<sub>99</sub> knot, the 10<sub>122</sub> knot, the 10<sub>144</sub> knot, the [[granny knot (mathematics)|granny knot]], and the composite knot 5<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;#&nbsp;5<sub>2</sub>.<ref>{{cite arXiv |eprint=0707.4210 |title=Sampling Lissajous and Fourier knots |year= 2007 |class=math.GT |last1=Boocher |first1=Adam |last2=Daigle |first2=Jay |last3=Hoste |first3=Jim |last4=Zheng |first4=Wenjing }}</ref>  In addition, it is known that every [[twist knot]] with [[Arf invariant]] zero is a Lissajous knot.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Hoste | first1=Jim | last2=Zirbel | first2=Laura |eprint=math.GT/0605632|title=Lissajous knots and knots with Lissajous projections |year=2006}}</ref>

== Symmetry ==
Lissajous knots are highly symmetric, though the type of symmetry depends on whether or not the numbers <math>n_x</math>, <math>n_y</math>, and <math>n_z</math> are all odd.

=== Odd case ===
If <math>n_x</math>, <math>n_y</math>, and <math>n_z</math> are all odd, then the [[point reflection]] across the origin <math>(x,y,z)\mapsto (-x,-y,-z)</math> is a symmetry of the Lissajous knot which preserves the knot orientation.

In general, a knot that has an orientation-preserving point [[reflection symmetry]] is known as '''strongly positive [[amphicheiral knot|amphicheiral]]'''.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Przytycki |first=Jozef H. |arxiv=math/0405151 |chapter=Symmetric knots and billiard knots |title=Ideal Knots |series=Series on Knots and Everything |editor-first1=A. |editor-last1=Stasiak |editor-first2=V. |editor-last2=Katrich |editor-first3=L. |editor-last3=Kauffman |publisher=World Scientific |volume=19 |pages=374–414 |year=2004 |bibcode=2004math......5151P }}</ref> This is a fairly rare property: only seven [[prime knot]]s with twelve or fewer crossings are strongly positive amphicheiral (10<sub>99</sub>, 10<sub>123</sub>, 12a427, 12a1019, 12a1105, 12a1202, 12n706).<ref>See {{cite arXiv |eprint=2310.05106|title=Strongly positive amphicheiral knots with doubly symmetric diagrams |year=2023 |class=math.GT |last1=Lamm |first1=Christoph}} This article contains a complete list of prime strongly positive amphicheiral knots up to 16 crossings.</ref> Since this is so rare, ′most′ prime Lissajous knots lie in the even case.

=== Even case ===
If one of the frequencies (say <math>n_x</math>) is even, then the 180° rotation around the ''x''-axis <math>(x,y,z)\mapsto (x,-y,-z)</math> is a symmetry of the Lissajous knot.  In general, a knot that has a symmetry of this type is called '''2-periodic''', so every even Lissajous knot must be 2-periodic.

=== Consequences ===
[[Image:Lissajous knot with parameters (4, 5, 41, 0.01, 0.16).svg|thumb|350px|A Lissajous knot with three factors: <math>(n_x,n_y,n_z)=(4,5,41)</math>, <br> <math>(\phi_x,\phi_y)=(0.01,0.16)</math>]]
The symmetry of a Lissajous knot puts severe constraints on the [[Alexander polynomial]].  In the odd case, the Alexander
polynomial of the Lissajous knot must be a perfect [[square (algebra)|square]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Hartley | first1 = R. | last2 = Kawauchi | first2 = A | year = 1979 | title = Polynomials of amphicheiral knots | journal = Mathematische Annalen | volume = 243 | pages = 63–70 | doi=10.1007/bf01420207| s2cid = 120648664 }}</ref>  In the even case, the Alexander polynomial must be a perfect square [[modular arithmetic|modulo]] 2.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Murasugi | first1 = K. | year = 1971 | title = On periodic knots | journal = [[Commentarii Mathematici Helvetici]] | volume = 46 | pages = 162–174 | doi=10.1007/bf02566836| s2cid = 120483606 }}</ref>  In addition, the [[Arf invariant]] of a Lissajous knot must be zero.  It follows that:
* The [[trefoil knot]] and [[figure-eight knot (mathematics)|figure-eight knot]] are not Lissajous.
* No [[torus knot]] can be Lissajous.
* No [[fibered knot|fibered]] [[2-bridge knot]] can be Lissajous.
